What is a meta-material? Stop the wave

Below is a chain of masses connected by springs. The gold driver on the left shakes it at the frequency you choose, and a wave travels along the chain to the right.

Now switch on the meta-material: the masses in the middle section each get a small oscillator (a gold hexagon). Without it, the wave passes through untouched at every frequency. With it, frequencies close to the oscillators' own natural frequency are stopped: the resonators move against the chain and the wave dies out inside the section. This frequency range is called a band gap.

Try it: switch the meta-material on, then slide the frequency into the shaded band in the chart.

Interactive 2

Spin a unit cell

A meta-material is built by repeating a small unit cell over and over, like bricks in a wall. Engineers design the shape of that cell to get the behaviour they need: very light yet stiff, energy-absorbing, or able to block vibrations.

  • Honeycomb: the shape in our logo. Light and stiff, used in aircraft panels and sandwich structures.
  • Cubic: the simplest lattice, with struts only along the edges.
  • BCC (body-centred cubic): adds diagonal struts to the centre, a common choice for 3D-printed lattices.
  • Octet truss: struts arranged as tetrahedra and octahedra, among the stiffest lattices for its weight.

Switch on Repeat 2 × 2 × 2 to see how cells join into a larger block.

Explained

Glossary

Short explanations of the terms used across this website. Elsewhere on the site, terms with a dotted underline open the same explanation when you tap or hover over them.

Band gap
A range of frequencies in which waves cannot travel through a periodic or resonant material, so vibrations in that range are strongly attenuated.
Digital twin
A virtual model of a physical asset that is updated with measured data, so it mirrors the asset's current state and can predict its future behaviour.
Fatigue
Progressive damage caused by repeated (cyclic) loading. It can lead to cracking and failure even when each individual load is well below the material's static strength.
Finite element method
A numerical method that divides a structure into many small elements to compute how it deforms, vibrates or fails under load.
Local resonator
A small oscillator embedded in a material. Near its own natural frequency it moves against the host material and absorbs its motion, opening a band gap even at low frequencies.
Meta-material
An engineered material whose properties come from its designed internal architecture, the shape and arrangement of small building blocks, rather than from its chemical composition. This allows behaviour not found in ordinary materials, such as blocking waves in certain frequency ranges.
Meta-structure
Clusters of structures designed to control how vibrations and waves are transmitted.
Offshore wind
Wind turbines installed at sea, where winds are stronger and steadier than on land. They must withstand demanding loads from wind, waves and corrosion.
Phase-field model
A modelling approach that represents a crack as a smooth damage field rather than a sharp discontinuity, which makes complex crack growth easier to simulate.
Physics-informed AI
Machine-learning models constrained by known physical laws, so they need less data and give physically consistent predictions.
Secondment
A period a Doctoral Candidate spends at another partner organisation, often in industry, to gain complementary skills and experience.
Structural Health Monitoring (SHM)
Continuous or periodic assessment of a structure's condition using sensors and data analysis, to detect damage early and support maintenance decisions.
Uncertainty quantification
Methods that describe how uncertainty in inputs, such as loads, material properties or models, affects predictions, so results come with confidence bounds.
Vibration mitigation
Reducing unwanted vibrations of a structure, for example by damping, isolation or wave-blocking meta-materials, to extend its service life and improve safety.
Wave energy converter
A device that captures the energy of ocean surface waves and converts it into electricity.
